The Grey snapper (Lutjanus griseus) exhibits life-history traits typical of a slow-growing, long-lived lutjanid inhabiting subtropical and tropical reef environments. Females in this species attain puberty at a fork length of 32 cm [Lp = 32 cm], a size threshold that generally corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and the capacity for reproductive contribution to the spawning stock. Field surveys of mature individuals indicate that the maximum fork length ever recorded for this species is 89 cm [Li = 89 cm], a substantial size that places Lutjanus griseus among the larger members of its genus within the Caribbean basin. This ultimate length corresponds to an asymptotic wet body mass on the order of 9,100 grams [Wwi = 9,100 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions parameterized for the northern Gulf of Mexico stock. Such a large adult body size, combined with a relatively late onset of female maturity, suggests that the species invests heavily in somatic growth before diverting resources toward gamete production.

The average gonadosomatic index (GSI) is approximately 14% [GSI = approximately 14%] when measured at a water temperature of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C]. This relatively low index implies that spawning females allocate only a small fraction of their total body mass to ovarian tissue during a given reproductive cycle, consistent with an iteroparous strategy that spreads reproductive effort across multiple seasons. The protracted spawning season observed across much of the species range, which extends from late spring through early autumn, further supports the interpretation that Lutjanus griseus prioritizes steady, repeated reproductive contributions over a single, explosive spawning event. Such a strategy is common among large-bodied, territorial reef fishes that experience moderate levels of natural mortality.

Early life stages of Lutjanus griseus are characterized by a brief but energetically critical period of endogenous nutrition following chorion rupture. At a developmental temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C], the age at birth, defined as the interval from fertilization through the completion of yolk-sac absorption, is approximately 3 days [ab = approximately 3 days], representing the sum of a 27-hour hatching interval and a subsequent 45-hour period of yolk depletion. Newly emerged prolarvae possess a wet weight at birth of only 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a value derived from the mean egg diameter of 0.85 mm documented for the related species Lutjanus stellatus and calculated using the standard volumetric relationship for spherical teleost eggs. This minute initial mass reflects the energetic constraints of a small, pelagic egg and underscores the vulnerability of the yolk-sac larva during the transition to exogenous feeding. The rapid absorption of yolk reserves within a narrow thermal window is a critical determinant of early survival and recruitment success.

Lifespan potential in Lutjanus griseus is substantial, reflecting the species slow life-history pace and relatively low natural mortality rate among adult age classes. The maximum recorded lifespan for this species, observed in wild populations from the Florida Keys and the northern Gulf of Mexico, is 25 years [am = 25 years] when assessed under the prevailing thermal regime of 24.8 °C [T = 24.8 °C]. This longevity places Lutjanus griseus among the longer-lived members of the Lutjanidae, comparable to estimates reported for the mangrove red snapper (Lutjanus argentimaculatus) and the cubera snapper (Lutjanus cyanopterus). Extended lifespans in these taxa are thought to be facilitated by their occupation of structured reef habitats that provide refuge from predation, as well as by their generalist feeding ecology, which buffers against interannual variability in prey availability. The combination of late maturity, moderate fecundity, and long reproductive lifespan is consistent with a bet-hedging life-history strategy.

Comparative studies across lutjanid species reveal that the fork length at female puberty in Lutjanus griseus, which is 32 cm [Lp = 32 cm], is intermediate between the values reported for the smaller-bodied lane snapper (Lutjanus synagris) and the larger cubera snapper (Lutjanus cyanopterus). This pattern suggests that the onset of sexual maturation in the genus is tightly linked to asymptotic body size, with larger species generally delaying maturity to accommodate extended somatic growth. Indeed, the ultimate fork length of 89 cm [Li = 89 cm] observed in Lutjanus griseus is nearly three times the size at which females first become reproductively active, indicating a prolonged juvenile phase dedicated largely to mass accumulation and habitat establishment. The spacing between size at puberty and maximum size may provide a demographic buffer against recruitment variability, as older, larger females contribute disproportionately to the egg pool across multiple spawning seasons. Such life-history features are important considerations for fisheries management.
